claims.text: The protective coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy microstructure.
The FCC and BCC phases have coherent, well-bonded interfaces.
Coherent FCC/BCC interfaces are strong barriers to dislocation motion.
Dislocations generated in the more ductile FCC phase are impeded at the FCC/BCC interfaces.
Dislocation blockage at the interfaces produces dislocation pile-ups.
Interfacial dislocation pile-ups generate an internal backstress.
The internal backstress reduces the effective driving force for continued creep deformation.
The interface-mediated backstress mechanism enhances creep resistance.
Compared with a comparable single-phase coating or a dual-phase coating with incoherent interfaces, the coherent FCC/BCC coating will exhibit lower creep strain under identical test conditions.
Compared with the baseline, the coherent FCC/BCC coating will exhibit a slower creep rate.
Post-test microscopy will reveal enhanced dislocation accumulation at FCC/BCC junctions.
The coherent FCC/BCC coating will show less evidence of grain-boundary sliding or diffusional creep.
A baseline without effective dislocation-barrier interfaces will have higher creep strain and faster creep rates.
The proposed mechanism operates primarily where dislocation-mediated creep predominates, such as at intermediate temperature and sustained high stress.
Testing at approximately 60–70% of yield strength and below the diffusion-creep regime is proposed to access the relevant deformation regime.
The mechanism may cease to govern when diffusional creep or catastrophic plastic instability becomes active.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction may depend on interface coherency, phase volume fraction, and changes in interface chemistry during prolonged loading.

A controlled comparison will test coherent FCC/BCC coatings against either single-phase coatings or dual-phase coatings with intentionally incoherent interfaces under identical stress and temperature.
Creep strain, creep rate, interface coherency, dislocation density, and interfacial pile-ups will be measured using extensometry, strain mapping, diffraction, and high-resolution electron microscopy.
The hypothesis will be rejected if the coherent FCC/BCC coating shows neither a statistically lower creep strain or creep rate nor enhanced interfacial dislocation pile-ups relative to the baseline.
